utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, good morning to you Madam Registrar. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, ma'am. All the accused are here. Prosecution, Defence teams are all here, with the exception of Mr. Bourgon for Nikolic. Prosecution, it's Mr. McCloskey and Mr. Vanderpuye. Ms. Frease is already present in the courtroom, so I suppose, Ms. Nikolic, you will take over from where Mr. Bourgon left, and then we'll continue. Yes, Ms. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Ms. Frease. Good morning to my learned friends. I would like to put just a few more questions from tab 11 of the binder proving the authenticity and reliability of the intercepts. And I think that my colleague will help you because he will give you the documents so then you will be able to follow my questions. In order for the others to be able to follow the documents, I would like the assistance of e-court. These are documents P01250B. That's B/C/S, and P1250D. That's in English. That's an intercept. The document that the witness used to analyse this intercept is P00334, and it's a combat report of the 18th of July, 1995. Ms. Frease, we just want to see the intercept in English in e-court. I assume that you were able to see this intercept which, according to the information that we have, was intercepted on the 18th of July at 1458 hours between unidentified speakers?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I can just refer to the index to double-check that time. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And you also have the document that you referred to in the analysis of this intercept, and that's the interim combat report of the 18th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: If we look at the intercept, the transcript of it, the last sentence of item 2 from one of the interim combat reports is mentioned, the one that is in front of you now; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Locations are mentioned, Petkovici, Baljkovica, Memici.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And the speakers are unidentified. They're marked as X and Y. And in this intercept, in line eight it says Petkovici, Baljkovica, Memici, referring to the interim combat report P00334; is that correct? And that it's the last sentence of item 2 of the document that was attached to this intercept?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And those are the contents of the intercept. If we turn to the document which was used to confirm the intercept in your analysis now, it's combat report of the 18th of July, 1995, which, if we look at the contents, it refers to only one sentence from the intercept, one sole sentence.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, I probably shouldn't agree so quickly. I -- do you want to give me a minute to read through the whole intercept? Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Of course. Of course.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: If we analyse the material that was used to confirm the intercept, you -- when you look at the document again, it's not possible to establish the identity of the participants; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: It's not possible to establish where the speakers were?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And you don't know which units they belonged to?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And does it fit the general time frame if we look at the report and the intercept? According to the information, the report was issued at 1317 hours, and the intercept was caught at 1458 hours. So then we can talk about the same time frame more or less; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: The contents of the document -- the words in the document are not identical to the words used in the intercept; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. Not at all. In fact, there's a lot of clarification mostly going on in the intercept between the location of Petkovci and Petkovici and so it's going back and forth about where the front line is, and that's the -- the content, the primary content of the intercepted conversation.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And what about the point and the objective of this intercept? Is that known?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say trying to identify, you know, more specifically the difference between Petkovci and Petkovici and the front line area. Baljkovica, Memici.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And towards the end of the conversation one of the speaker's notes that there is a mistake, a typo, while the report was being typed out, a teleprinter typo.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what they said, that there must have been a mistake on the teleprinter when it came out, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: But you will agree with me that this intercept does not provide anything more than is already contained in the attached report or document?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. I mean -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Did you ever talk with any of the users of the information that was coming from the intercepts or, rather, did you ever have contact with members of the 2nd Corps or other units of the B and H army that used these intercepts?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you be more specific about what you -- who you mean by "users"?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I mean those persons or those units to whom reports of intercepts were sent to and who received the information from the conversation. I'm not referring to any specific person. I can refer to units of the B and H army whose members intercepted these conversations. Did you ever contact any persons who received reports of these intercepts, units, the end users of this information in terms of checking the authenticity or veracity of the documents?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember speaking with one commander, yes. I don't remember whether we had a specific conversation about him having received information from the 2 Corps about communication that was intercepted.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And could those conversations be defined as checking on the authenticity of the intercepts as one of the additional ways of checking on the source documents that you used?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could give you an example of -- of something like that, but then I would need to mention the name of the commander, and I think probably closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And that was the point in time when you checked on the reliability of the information with one of the end users of that information?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's an example, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I have no further questions. Thank you, Ms. Frease.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you so much, Madam Nikolic. Who is going next? Madam Fauveau. You've asked for two and a half hours.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There are still another two Defence teams that wish to cross-examine the witness. Let me just check with them. The Gvero team, you asked for 20 minutes. Do you stand by that?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We'll need that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the Popovic team?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 30 minutes. So that would bring us, if you stick to your two hours 30 minutes to three hours 40 minutes, and we'll barely make it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, do you need 30 minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. My cross-examination will refer only to documents that were given to me in the meantime by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Yes, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, when you were working you were listening to -- you were talking to many people who were intercepting conversations. When you got in touch with interceptors that with operators who were members of the army of the BiH, did the officer of the army have to be present at the -- at the interview?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean a commanding officer, a superior to the operator?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: What I would like to know is, an officer of the army of BiH, independently of the fact if it was a superior officer, did they require that somebody from the army be present during that interview?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether anyone was present during the very first interview, I don't recall. But I do recall, very clearly, a conversation that we had with the commanding officer of the 2 Corps when we were discussing having access to the operators, and that the -- the general answer to your question is no, there were no -- no officers of the ABiH present during the interviews with the operators. And when we inquired, asked, whether there were any areas that were off limits, in our questioning, we were told no, that they had full -- had been given full authority to tell us everything that they knew.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: However, there were situations where officers of the BiH were present at interviews or during those interviews that you had.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you could provide me with specific examples of when they were present, I would be happy to look at them. As I said, it's possible that during the first interview, when we were getting going with the process, to understand the process, that someone other than the interviewee was present.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you agree with me that the presence of an officer of the BiH, during an interview, could have had some kind of influence on what the operator would tell you?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say, given the circumstances and given the fact that we were told by a commanding officer that there were no -- that there was not subject a matter that was off limits to us with respect to what we were inquiring about, without you giving me a very specific example, I would disagree.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown P2337, and I would like to go into private session for a few questions, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's do that. Let's go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Witness, if you were to read the statement today, eight years after this interview, would you be able to remember what the interviewee told you and what his superior told you?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: During the interview of the 25th of January, 2007, this is on transcript page 38 -- 6388 and 6389, you stated that during the interviews you had with the operator you said that certain procedures needed to be applied, i.e., the name -- the way in which the conversation were being recorded. Do you know whether the ABiH army had such a procedure, which was to regulate the way in which the recordings were conducted?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you be more specific with your question, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you know whether a specific rule existed with -- within the ABiH army, if there was a particular way of recording the conversations, the recordings, the transcripts, the way the reports were being sent, and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was certainly a procedure with respect to how the operator sat down at the tables where the UHER recording machines were, how they scanned the various channels with their headphones on. When they came across something, a conversation that sounded interesting, they would record it. At a certain point when they found the time then -- sorry, before -- at the time that they started to record the conversation they would note the time, and as I've explained before, often also the channel and the frequency but not always those three things.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I don't wish to interrupt you. I think there was a misunderstanding here. What I'm interested in is as follows: Do you know whether rules and regulations existed in writing whether such a recording needed to apply and comply with the procedure of the ABiH army?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of specific regulations. What I do recall is that they followed the standard procedures that the JNA, the Yugoslav national army, had previously used. But I don't know whether that -- whether that applies to the recording, the capturing of that information, or the processing of the information.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you know that the JNA had written a regulation as regards the recording of conversations?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: And when you say recording of conversations, you mean when they sat down at the desk to ...

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: What I have in mind is comprehensive regulation, the way in which the recording needed to be conducted, the way in which the transcript needed to be taken, and the way in which the reports were being forwarded?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And you didn't reckon it was necessary to say whether such regulations existed when you heard that the ABiH army was by and large adopting the same procedures as the JNA?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: When you put the question like that I can't say that I didn't reckon it was necessary, but I -- I'm not aware of such documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You said -- this was on the 25th of January, 2007, on page 2374. You stated that sometimes the time that was shown in the book didn't quite tally with the time that was mentioned in the report, and you said that sometimes the person who typing up the report changed the times. Did you ask why the person who was typing up the conversation had changed the time?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be very specific, I would need to look at that typist's statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Ma'am, I don't think you referred to a particular statement when you said that the person who was typing up the conversation changed the time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you could give the page number again. 25th of January.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 34 -- 6394. 25th of January, 2007.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Still, we are where we -- where the witness left it. You are being specific, and she is telling you that in order to give you a specific answer she would have to consult the statement of the witness relating to that particular document, if there is one.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's a question I'm asking. I don't now which statement we're talking about, because in the report no particular statement is mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sir. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Perhaps it might be more useful if my learned friend could read back to the witness the precise context in the statement that she made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I think that's a good suggestion. Madam Fauveau, could you do that, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: So you talked about the time discrepancies, and the question, that was put to you by the Prosecutor and put to you again by Your Honour, ran as follows: "In preparation for such discrepancies, as Mr. Vanderpuye has referred to them, which was acceptable enough to you to reach certain conclusions?" [Interpretation] And you -- your question was yes. And after that Your Honour put the following question to you: [In English] "And what were these explanations, if you could remember?" [Interpretation] And you answered: [In English] "Well, simply that that -- and it was one -- it was one typist in particular who -- who changed the times a little bit from the time of the actual recording to the time that he actually typed it up." [Interpretation] What I would like to know is this: Do you remember the name of this person? Without giving us the name, just whether you remember the name of this person? Did this person provide any plausible explanation for the change?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember the name of the person.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And if we were to move into private session, could you give us this name, please?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's go into private session for a short time, please. And you haven't answered the second part of the question, whether this person provided you with any plausible explanation for the change.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You have just said that the time difference was due to the difference in time of the recording and the time at which the conversation was typed up, but if we turn to the report of the 25th of January, 2007, that is to page 6394, the time differential is one minute or five minutes? Are you saying that one or five minutes is enough time for the operator to record the conversation, to listen to it several times over, and to write it down in the book or the logbook?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I gave that as an example of some of the discrepancies, as some of the differences that one could find between them. I think to further clarify that, it would be best to speak with the person who was responsible for doing that work.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Isn't it fair to say that the person who was typing up the report had to type out exactly what the operator had written down word-for-word?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the procedure, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: So the operator who was changing the time was breaching the rules and regulations, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose. You know, I mean it didn't happen all the time. There were examples -- there are examples where it did happen, but yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: When you conducted your investigation, did you ever discover what happened to the reports when they reached the 2nd Corps? Were they printed out? Were they recorded? What happened to them?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: They went to the intelligence section for analysis, and then ones that analysts considered to be relevant they moved on -- or they forwarded to other units, for example.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you know whether these reports were recorded in a logbook when they reached the command?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: As part of your job, in 1998, you had an opportunity to visit Sector North and Sector South.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: When you were on Sector North, this is what I'm interested in for the moment, you were able to say what kind of technical equipment was available there at the time you went there; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And this equipment was photographed; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And this equipment was described to you as the type of equipment that had been used during the war, i.e., in July 1995; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Did you have a way of checking whether this equipment had been used in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the information that we received from the ABiH personnel who accompanied us, and in Mr. Hunter's reports, he talks about the equipment, and I think it's best to refer to his report.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sure, but what I'm interested in is how he was able to establish that this was the same equipment as the equipment that had been used in 1995, because that is in effect what he says in his report. Notwithstanding the information you got from the army personnel of the ABiH army, were you able to confirm this information any other way?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: It's okay. I was going to object. I withdraw the objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, you can answer the question, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Exemplars were taken from the various UHER machines that were up there. Beyond that, I can't comment on the technical aspects of the machinery.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Would you agree to say that nothing enables you to establish that the equipment that was photographed was the same equipment that was used in Sector North in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. If I could add one -- one thing, which is that taking exemplars off of machines, well, they're apparently like fingerprints, but I don't have the technical capability of commenting on them further.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: During this on-site visit in Sector North, did you check this out? Did you try to listen to the conversation that came from the same direction as the conversations that were being intercepted by the ABiH army in 1995?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: So as far as Sector South is concerned, you discovered, when you conducted your investigation, that after the Dayton Accords, this had been closed down and the equipment had been transferred to Sector North; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I believe the site was closed down in December of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And do you remember that at the time you visited Sector South, an ABiH army officer told you there was no equipment left in Sector South? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't -- I don't remember that specifically. I remember him saying that a lot of the equipment -- I think he said that the equipment had been transferred to the north but that also, I think, that some of the equipment had been returned to people because it had been requisitioned from them during the war. But I believe that we took photographs of equipment there. I don't have a firm memory of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Yes. You did see some of the equipment, the UHER equipment in Sector South. What I'm interested is this: These UHER equipment, how come they were all of a sudden in Sector South at the time you were there?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: We're able to have a look at this equipment, UHER equipment, which is the same type of equipment that the operators used during the war, and you said at the hearing of the 25th of January, 2007, that this UHER equipment could wind the tape back and could record over old recordings; is that right? What I'm interested in is this: Could you wind the tape back, and could you simply wipe out the old conversations?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you asking whether there's a distinction between erasing the type and recording over it?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I'm asking you whether one can -- whether the recording machine could establish this distinction?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: So at any rate, you said that a new recording could be made over an old recording. Do you know that in certain cases -- or there were some cases in which the new recording wasn't good enough and, therefore, some of the old conversations could be heard, that two conversations were overlapping, in other words?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's been a while since I've listened to a bunch of recordings, and not being a technical person, I hesitate to answer your question. I'm just not sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Can we show witness Exhibit 5D172, please. [In English] It's the document 5D172. [Interpretation] Could we see the beginning of the last sentence on this document. The first sentence before the conversation, the short introduction that the members of the police were always. Can you read this. [In English] "Did not erase the last conversation properly so this one was almost inaudible."

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: When you -- when you analysed the intercepts, did you bear this in mind? Did you account for the fact that there were -- there could be two overlapping conversations?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember that it -- it factored in to -- to the analysis. I would just point out at the top of this document, I think it was a document that was taken over from 2 Corps, if you could scroll back up to the top of the document. It's not right -- it's not an SDB document. It's a 2 Corps -- it's a 2 Corps document that was taken over from the SDB -- or -- that was taken over by the SDB. I mean, it's just a detail, but ...

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Thank you for having clarified this. Could we now turn to document 5D150, please.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I guess I would also just point out that when there were sort of discrepancies like this where it wasn't possible to hear one of the participants very well or that the rest of the conversation wasn't recorded or that the operators considered that a certain part of the conversation wasn't important, they made notations like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Yes. This is true, but how can one be sure that when this should have been noted down it wasn't noted down? Perhaps sometimes these annotations were missing.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. But they really are present on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Don't answer that question. Move to the next question, Madam Fauveau, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: As far as document 5D150 is concerned, which you have before you, this document mentions steel battery. There's a mistake in the English text, so please look at the B/C/S text. This text mentions a steel battery that prior to that time had belonged to the United Nations and which was used in Sector South. At the time you visited Sector South, were you able to see the batteries on this site and whether they were still there?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't read the whole document, but I wouldn't have known what -- I'm not sure I would have known what I was looking at.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: It's the fourth sentence. Second sentence in the second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would object at this point. I think the witness has already answered the question. She has indicated she doesn't have any familiarity with the batteries or what they would appear to be or ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In a way I think she has, Madam Fauveau, because previously she said, "I wouldn't have known -- I'm not sure I would have known what I was looking at." Yes, but irrespective of reading. In other words, reading the document was not going to educate her more there.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: In the course of the interviews you had with the operator or during your on-site visit, did you understand what the various jobs of the units were, those who were intercepting the conversations? Did they have to do anything else other than intercept the conversations?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Their primary job was to intercept conversations, but they also had to cook and clean and take care of the facility.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I'm sure they did that, but that was not the purpose of my question. Did you realise that they were also in charge of scrambling and interfering with the enemy transmissions?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: When you took charge of the logbooks or these second logbooks, 135 onwards, did you not notice that some of these books had nothing to do with intercepts but had to do with information on scrambling of the conversations?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't have a memory of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Could we now -- could the witness be shown Exhibit number 5D193, please. This is a logbook which you prepared, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Could we move to page 4, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have numbers 185 and 186, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it fair to say that the two notebooks refer to the scrambling of the conversations?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They both say "jamming unit."

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And do you know from what site these two notebooks came?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not without looking at the notebooks, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And do you know whether the unit to which the notebooks referred was a separate unit or was it part of the unit that intercepted the conversations?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the right question. I don't know the answer to that question, but I -- I mean, I could guess, but without --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Don't guess.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Don't guess, yes. I'd have to look at the notebooks.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And do you know, and I don't ask you to guess but really to refer to what you know, is it possible to scramble conversations on a site and to listen to those same conversations on the same site?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you should ask -- I'm sure there are other people who are more competent than I to answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to show to the witness Exhibit 5D189.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Again, no broadcast, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I would request that the document not be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Witness, is this a report that you drafted?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Could we look at page 4 of the document, please. It's the penultimate paragraph, and I will read out part of the report. It's fairly technical terminology, but perhaps you might be of assistance. "[In English] As explained, when the JNA withdrew in May 1992, they took with them the most modern tactical communication equipment and in essence left the VRS with early 1950's technology equipment. At the same time, the VRS did not have the capability to 'manufacture' encipher fills for the equipment, and apparently Belgrade was unwilling or unable to provide the necessary fills to allow the multi-channel network to operate in a secure mode." [Interpretation] I must admit that I do not understand a thing. I mean, I don't understand a thing to this technical language. So I would like to ask you, does this mean that the person who communicated this information to you thought that the army of the Republika Srpska did not have the possibility or did not use secure communication methods?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I take a minute and just read the full paragraph and maybe even the preceding paragraph, if you wouldn't mind moving it up just a little.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'm own going to object to the question insofar as it calls for what was -- what someone else thought. I don't know the witness's capacity is to answer that. As to what they said, that's a different issue all together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You would have been right if this had not been the report that Ms. Frease had prepared. This is a report that Ms. Frease prepared, so the question is perfectly legitimate.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. If I can now just go back to your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Well, come back to the paragraph that you read in detail. Does this mean that the army of Republika Srpska did not have the means to use secure communication methods?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: What it means to me is that they had a problem with secure methods. However, when looking at the intercepted communication, there are many references to the fact that the lines, that they were communicating on, were not secure and that certain conversations needed to be transmitted on secure lines. So I don't know for what period of time this information, the information that was given to me by this particular person, would have held.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: But did you check with the various units of the Republika Srpska, namely with the army of the Republika Srpska, what communication methods they had and whether they had a secure mode of communication or not?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't have that opportunity.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: So you don't know whether the information communicated to you by the officer of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina was exact, was correct?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was reporting what he had told me.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: On the 27th of February, on page 11 of the transcript, you said that you only know where the documents containing the intercepted conversations were found. Does this mean that you did not know where the diskettes, the -- the notebooks, the printed matter, the audiotapes were stored during three years as of July 1995 till March, April, or even later, when they were passed on to you?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I have some sense of what we were told about where the documents, in particular, the notebooks, had been kept in the intervening time.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Very well. I will come back to the notebooks a little bit later, but I'd like to ask you whether it is true that you received all of this material in Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the notebooks -- depends a little bit what you -- exactly what you mean. It's where we took possession of the material, but it's not where the material -- specifically with respect to the notebooks, it's not where they were found.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Let me specify my question. Is it true that you took possession of all the material in Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's also not quite -- quite accurate. Some of the tapes we took possession of in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Thank you for specifying that. With regard to the written documents, the printed documents, the report and the notebooks, and perhaps also the floppy disks, were those documents handed over to the OTP in Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And do you know whether all the official documents of the army of BiH were archived in Sarajevo in 1996?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, could we again move to private session for a couple of questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's do that. Let's move into private session for a couple of questions and then revert back to open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it fair to say that before you -- well, in fact you already answered that question, so I'll reformulate it. When the notebooks were found in the northern sector, is it fair to say that they were found in a -- in a warehouse where other goods were stored and weapons as well?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether it's a translation issue or not. I wouldn't call it a warehouse. It was their facility. I wasn't present, but what I recall is that it was -- they were found in a basement office of that facility, of the northern facility. And it's possible that there were other things there that you mention.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Did you carry out an investigation to know who might have had access to the notebooks during the period between 1995 and 1998?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: My recollection of the path that the notebooks took was that when the -- when they were picked up from the various sites, they were taken to the location where the commander at the time had his office. And then when he moved offices, they were taken with him there, which is where they were found at the northern site.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: With regard to the room in which the notebooks were found, do you know who had access to that room?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it was the site commander. Or I don't know to the room specifically, actually. I think that to the -- to the locker where they were found, that it was the commander, the site commander, who had had access to it.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it fair to say that when the members of the OTP saw the notebooks for the first time, and I'm referring to the time when the notebooks were in no particular order, is it true that at that time the representatives of the OTP did not study the notebooks?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's my understanding. Again, I wasn't there, but right. I believe they skimmed through them enough to -- to see what the contents were generally.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And when the representatives of the OTP arrived on site a few days later, those notebooks were in a good order?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: They weren't [realtime transcript read in error "were"] in the same shape that they had been found in, right.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And when the representatives of the OTP saw the notebooks for the first time, they did not take any pictures of them. They did not annotate them in any way, they did not mark them in any way. Is that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: How did you know, and I'm referring not to you personally but referring to the OTP, that the notebooks that were found, in a very neat order, on -- the second time were the same notebooks that had been seen the first time in disorder?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise to interrupt Madam Fauveau, but I believe the answer of the witness was misinterpreted. It's on page 29, line 4. The answer of the witness was they were not in the same shape that they had been found in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're hundred per cent right and I heard her say that. Thank you. The transcript will be corrected accordingly, Mr. Lazarevic. So, Ms. Frease, do you need the question to be put to you again, or I suppose you can answer. You have the transcript in front of you. You can answer it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When members of the OTP came back the second time and found the notebooks and asked why they had been sort of tidied up, the commander said that he had been embarrassed that they had been found in so much disorder, and therefore he tried to make some order out of them. But to your question of how do we know that they were exactly the same notebooks, we don't other than the commander of the site said so and gave the reason for trying to organise them.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: When you received, personally, these notebooks, were they dusty?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Were they damaged by moisture?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember them being musty, but I don't -- yeah, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you not find that notebooks that were stored for three years in a basement should have been dusty and musty and, at any rate, damaged to some extent?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Don't answer that question, please, Ms. Frease. Next question, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You said during the hearing of the 19th of January, 2007, that the OTP first received the printed matter, then the notebooks, and finally the audiotapes in the electronic versions. The 19th of January, page 6088. When you referred to the printed matter or printed material, were you referring to the binders containing 550 pages?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And you received those binders in April 1998?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I believe we received those -- I had thought that we had received them in March, but we received them in April along with the notebooks and along with the tapes, because we hadn't -- I think what happened was that we didn't have the authorisation from the ministry -- from the defence ministry of the ABiH in March, which is why we weren't allowed to take possession of those items until our next mission in April.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: During the hearing of January 25, 2007, at page 6360, you said that the printed matter was an analytic tool used by the ABiH army and that the army had withdrawn some information in order to analyse the material with greater ease. Do you remember making that statement?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Withdrawn some of the information, I assume you mean the headers and that sort of -- that sort of information. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I -- go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you know who was the person who created the printed matter in the form in which you received it? Was this a member of the police or a member of the army?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the army, a member of the army.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you know who that person was?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And do you know when those documents were, in fact, established in the form in which you saw them, were they the documents that were prepared to be submitted to the OTP, or had they already been prepared beforehand?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe those were documents that had been prepared for the OTP. The cover sheet that -- I believe it was Mr. Zivanovic showed me -- I think had a date of the 3rd of March or something like that on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any time it's convenient for you, we can have a 25-minute break, but you've still got another two minutes, but I don't know if --

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I'll just finish off with this particular matter. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: If you know that they were not the documents that were prepared during the war, those documents in the form that you received them, and if you know that some information in fact was withdrawn, was taken out, even if you know that it was just, let's say, formal information that was taken out, how can you be sure that the content of the conversations was not modified by the person who prepared these printouts for you?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we couldn't be, and that's why it was important that we process every -- every version of the conversations that we were given. So we first took the information that we were given in the printouts -- I've explain this before, and I -- but we first took that information, those 550 pages and processed every conversation in it. And that material dated from, I believe, the 9th of July to the 31st of July, and there were close to 1.200 conversations there. After we had processed that and we had the notebooks, then we took the notebooks and we processed the notebooks, comparing the notebooks, the conversations and the information that was contained within the notebooks and compared it to the information that was contained within the printouts. And then subsequently, when we received all of these diskettes and now with the electronic versions of these conversations, we were further able to cross-reference. So it really was a -- was a process of cross-referencing, cross-referencing, cross-referencing.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You said earlier that you think the printed matter, the printouts, were prepared for you after the war then, I assume. Do you then today consider that these printouts were not authentic material dating from 1995?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Can you explain to me how you can at the same time state that -- at the same time that it was material prepared specifically for you and yet at the same time that it dated from 1995?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you look at only that material and you took only that, then -- then, yes. You know, I agree one would have a lot of questions. But I think it's really important to take all of this material together, and then not only taking the various versions of the material, the printed, the notebooks, the electronic versions, but then going through and further establishing and corroborating the contents of those conversations with other sources.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I just have one last question before the break. I agree with you that of course you have to look at the whole, but before analysing all of the material comprehensively, do you not have to be sure that each element in itself is authentic?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had many doubts about this material when we first picked it up. We didn't know whether -- whether it was authentic. And it was only through going through the process over and over and over again and cross-referencing it and cross-referencing it over a period of years that we gained the confidence of the contents, the authenticity, and the reliability of the material.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, could we now take the break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Fauveau. We'll have a 25-minute break starting from now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Just before the break, Witness, we were talking about the measures that you took in order to obtain the documents. You explained us that you doubted the authenticity of that material. Since you had doubts, wasn't it simpler to send the material, and I'm talking about notebooks, to an expert who would be able to trace back the ink and the paper?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: We first wanted to know what the contents of that material was, and that was our primary focus. Whether -- if the material didn't contain anything that was of relevance, you know, then taking the step that you suggest probably would have been premature. But we did not, in fact, to my knowledge, send the notebooks to a handwriting or an ink analyst.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's make this clear. That was during your time here. You don't know what could have happened afterwards; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: During the hearing of the 2nd of March, 2007, you mentioned some dates, and you told us that it was very important for you to date the intercepted conversations. Is it exact to say that when you received those notebooks, you tried to put a date on those intercepts?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We tried to date the intercepts, whether it was through the printed material we first received or through the notebooks.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: During the 2nd March, 2007 hearing, on page 63 of the transcript, you said that the intercepts were not transcribed in their chronological order. I would like to know, when did you conclude that those intercepts were not transcribed in their chronological order?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that that would have become clear once we started taking interviews from the operators. So about a year later.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: But when you testified in the Krstic trial on the 22nd of March, 2001, page 8947, you've stated that those transcripts were written in their chronological order. Can you now explain to us what this discrepancy means?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it would be helpful if it were possible for us to take specific examples, but I can -- I can give you a sort of general example of -- of how that kind of a discrepancy might have occurred, which is that in the -- with the reference that you make to my statement in the Krstic trial in 2001, it's possible that the conversations that were contained within the printed material, that is the 550 pages, were in an order, a more chronological order, than the order that was found within the notebooks.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Again, in the Krstic trial you mentioned notebooks, and you stated on page 8947: [In English] "these were recorded chronologically from the morning to the evening. In most cases where it changed over from night to morning we considered that to be the beginning of a new day." [Interpretation] Can you explain that statement, since Friday you've told us that those intercepts were not necessarily transcribed in their chronological order?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's as I explained it on Friday, that when the intercept operators sat down at the table -- at their tables, they noted the time, the frequency, and the channel that the conversation was coming in on. Sometimes there were many conversations that were coming in, so they had their headphones on. They were listening. They were noting down those pieces of information that I just mentioned, again not always all three of them, and they would continue to record conversations. Once there was a lull, they would then go back and begin to transcribed the conversations. So it wasn't necessarily the case that they would start from the first conversation that they had noted and work down through to the end, the last conversation that they had noted. Sometimes they considered that a particular conversation was more -- of more importance, so they would transcribe that conversation first. They might even send it separately, in a separate report, as we've seen marked urgent or priority, and then they would go through and they would transcribe those other conversations. And that's how it's possible to account for some jumping around, I guess, in times within a day.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Very well. But my first question is why didn't you say that when you testified in the Krstic trial?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I think it might be useful if my learned colleague could put to the witness the question and the response in the Krstic case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In the Krstic case. I fully agree. Do you have the reference handy, Ms. Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I just read the entire portion that I referred to. It's page 8947 of the transcript of the 27th of March, 2001. If you would like it, I could re-read the portion that I just read.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Could you also read the question that was put to the witness in the Krstic trial, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: "And could you tell the Trial Chamber who assisted or not, who assisted you, how long it took you to fully analyse and date these particular intercepts and the methodology that you used in doing so?"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Are you in a position to answer the question now, Ms. Frease?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I feel like I'm still missing some context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is there anything else in the transcript from the Krstic trial that the witness said in relation to this point, either questions before or after that is relevant? We don't have the text, the transcript here in front of us, so -- unless -- unless --

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, Mr. President, but it's an answer that's more than two pages long, and I'll start another -- I'll ask another question, because the only portion that was referring to the notebook, I just read it to her.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I think you better move to your next question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it right to say that when you would find a date in the notebook you would consider that a date to be a confirmed date, a correct date?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Now, whether there is an exception to that, that's a possibility, but in general, yes, we did consider those firm dates.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Did you ever consider the possibility that the person who wrote down a date may have made a mistake?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This question has been asked and been asked. Do you wish to answer if again, Ms. Frease? I think everyone has asked you this question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can answer it again if you'd like me to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead and try to go through it as fast as you can, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And did you put down the conversations, the intercepts for which you thought there was a date -- mistake in the date?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When we had a doubt about a date, we recorded it in normal font on the index that we created initially to process these intercepts. Once we considered that the date was a firm date, then we bolded that date.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with you. But isn't it right that when you would find a date that was written down in the notebook, because you also had intercepts without a date, you would consider that date whenever you would find a date to be a firm date?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Again, you know, unless there was -- unless there was some reason or there was some -- some other -- you know, some discrepancy or something that made us unsure about that, but, yes. In most cases, yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: During your deposition of the 27th of February, 2007, page 4750, that the captain who was in charge of putting the dates at the beginning of a conversation in the notebook told you not to take into account the dates that are written down in the notebook -- notebooks. Did the captain explain to you why you were not to trust those dates?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me just clarify a little bit what you say in -- in your statement, in your question. We're referring -- when I -- when I mentioned the captain, I was referring to the registration numbers that he recorded at the front of the notebook, and then he would record a date there. So that's the date that we're talking about. We're not talking about the dates inside the notebooks that the operators wrote down. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, exactly. That's what I'm asking you.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. The reason that he told us -- told me not to -- well, to -- let me rephrase it. The reason that he said that those dates were not necessarily relevant to the conversations that were contained within the notebook was that those were -- they're internal registration numbers and dates that he would have recorded that notebook as being a notebook that would be used at one of the sites where the operators were working.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Yes, I understand the meaning of those dates, but I do not understand why did he tell you not to trust those dates.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't that we weren't supposed to trust the dates. It's that those were his dates. For example, that would have been the date that he would have recorded in his records that that notebook maybe was going to go to a particular site. It didn't mean that that was the day that the operators at that site would begin to use that notebook.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: But the dates that he would put in, the registration dates, were those the right dates? Were those dates accurate? Did they really reflect the dates when those notebooks were registered?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye? Okay. Go ahead. Answer the question, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I guess I feel like that's a question that should be put to him. I don't know. Those were the dates that he wrote down in his registration log. I don't recall seeing his log and making a comparison between those dates and his log, if he had a log.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown notebook 22, please. It's the notebook with the ERN number 00804523. And for the transcript, in e-court, it's Exhibit P2336. Could the witness be shown the page which ends with 4537, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And no broadcast, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown the transcript on the 16th of July, 16th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you know who put that date down?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And when you talked to the operators, you never tried to find out who wrote that date down?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have a specific recollection about that date, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And do you know when that date was put down?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you know why it was circled?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Could we take the page which ends with 4610, please. Could the -- could the page be scrolled down, please - thank you - to see the crossed-out section. Good. Do you agree that the portion that's crossed out is in fact a date?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And do you know who put that date on that page?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You also don't know who crossed it out?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Can you read, however, the date that's there?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It says the 23/7/1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Could it be -- would it be possible to see 4707, please, the last page.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: 4607; correction.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you see on that page the date 23rd of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And you do not know who put that date down or when it was written down?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that that date and the date of the 16th of July, as well as the date of the 23rd of July that had been crossed out, could have been written down once the notebooks were in the possession of the OTP?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: How can you say that with such certainty?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because members of the Office of the Prosecutor did not write in these notebooks.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: But you do know that representatives of the OTP can make mistakes, and there was an OTP representative that put a teleprinter number in one of the pages of the notebook?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: She's answered that question. Let's move to the next, Madam Fauveau, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Witness, can you confirm with absolute certainty that those dates were not written down after 1995 and before the OTP took possession of those notebooks? So between March 1995 and the time when the OTP took possession of those notebooks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: The question's been put, and the witness has already answered that she doesn't know when the dates were put in the book, who put them in, or who circled them, or anything of that nature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. We agree with that, Mr. Vanderpuye. So your next question, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You told us that the electronic version that you received later helped you to date conversations, and you said that on the 27th of February, on the transcript page 52. Is it right that what helped you to date conversations is reports that bore a number and a date?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you referring to the electronic versions of those conversations?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I'm referring to reports that were complete. So reports that have the name of the person, who sent them, who received them, the dates, et cetera. I'm not really interested in the electronic versions or the other types of versions, but those kinds of reports.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have the transcript up, so I'm just going to re-read your question. I think it's probably better if you quote back to me exactly what I said. But in principle, the electronic versions further confirmed the dates that we had confirmed earlier. So it was a sort of triple check to dates that we had had before.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you for that answer. But I would like to know is it not right to say that the first report, so I'm talking about the reports that had the name of the person who was to get it, the name of the person who sent the report, the date, et cetera, you received them first in March of 1998?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I would like to know, if you can recall, if the first documents containing intercepts, if those were the June and July reports of 1995, but that the complete reports on paper containing the name of the sender, the name of the recipient, the date, the number, and the intercept with all the data that go with it?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm still not sure I understand. The first reports we received were in July of 1995, those 550 pages from the 9th of July through the 31st of July. Some of those reports contained initials at the bottom of the reports, I believe. They didn't mean a lot to us at that point. Certainly not all of the conversations in those reports contained dates. With respect to the name of the recipient, the number, and the intercept with all the data that goes with it, there I assume you're talking about the electronic versions of the reports which were then received later after I had left the OTP with the exception of those two diskettes that we had received in April of 1999 that we were unable to open.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: The binder of 550 documents, you received it in April 1998. That's what you said. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And those printouts did not contain any additional information with regard to the conversations that are written down in the notebooks?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they did contain a bit of additional information in that the police, the SDB reports were included within those 550 pages.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Could we please stick to the reports of the army.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that's correct, with the exception of the fact that I think that there -- that some of the initials of the operators and the typists might have been included in some of those reports, and they might also have included some additional dates, but I'm not -- I'm not certain about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And the notebooks also sometimes contained the initials of the person, either who had typed them up or who had recorded the conversation; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now show the witness Exhibit 5D189.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are not -- at least I speak for myself, but Judge Prost, I think, and Judge Kwon, are not receiving any interpretation. I'm sorry, Madam Fauveau, but I suppose you need to repeat a little bit. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, I would like to request that the document not be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. And I would appreciate if all of you, you do that, because you alert us beforehand. I appreciate that very much, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: So it is the report that you drafted or note that you drafted in April 1998. Could we move to page 3 of the document. Could we show the part that starts with e-court, the entire paragraph, please. You see that you wrote in this note the following: "[In English] A complete record of messages can be found in the 'reports' which were sent to the 2nd Corps on a daily basis. These reports include all intercepts from those sites and not simply those relating to the Srebrenica investigation. Such reports covering June and July 1995 were given to ICTY team 6 during their March 1998 mission." [Interpretation] Do you belong to the sixth team?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And in this note you speak about daily reports. I'm sure that you had the opportunity while you were working for the OTP, that you had the opportunity to know what daily reports are within an army. Can you explain to me where those daily reports are today, because I have not seen a single one.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that what is meant by "daily reports" are the reports -- or the electronic versions of the transcribed conversations that were sent on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: However, with regard to the electronic versions, did you not say that they were received far later by the OTP?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And where are the reports that you received in March 1995 -- 1998?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there's a problem with the dates.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: But it's a note from April 1998, so apparently the reports were received before you drafted the note.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: And that could have been a mistake on my part. It would have been a reference to the -- the binder of 550 pages that -- again, I believe the cover sheet of that binder is dated the 3rd of March, 1998, but I don't believe that we actually received that binder, that the OTP actually took it into possession until the 24th of April, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: No, I don't think that it refers to that binder, because look at the next page, what is written on the next page. I'm sorry, the next sentence. It was my mistake. "[In English] 2nd Corps personnel took it upon themselves to extract the intercepts relating to the Srebrenica and compiled them in a binder totaling more than 300 pages. This binder was also given to ICTY personnel during the same mission."

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What mistake are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think -- I think it's a mistake that -- I mean, totaling more than 300 pages at the time. I don't think we knew that there were 550 pages. I think that both of these comments refer to the same body of material, and that in this will note, that this is incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Very well. That's what you think, and I understand that you can't remember. So reading the note today, quite clearly there are two different things, the reports and the binder containing a selection made by the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, though I think here the reports refer to the -- how can I explain this? The reports that were sent on a daily basis were the ones that we now know of as having headers, where when the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina compiled these reports, I think they're -- I think they were referring to the same reports. For them, it was the same -- it contained the same information, and that I used the language that they were using.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we show the witness Exhibit 5D191.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: If I'm not mistaken, this is a note that you also drafted. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Could we move to page 3 of that note. I will not read out paragraph 2 again. It contains exactly the same sentence as the one that I already read out in the other note. What I'm interested in is what comes after that paragraph, and you wrote the following: "[In English] However, it must be noted that due to large volume, not all intercepted conversations were sent to 2nd Corps each day. During a conversation with 2nd Corps personnel in March, Rick Butler was told that some messages from July may not have been sent in the form of a report until months later (in September, October or November). Therefore, we must eventually request reports from these later months as well." [Interpretation] What I'm interested in is if some reports were sent later, how can one be sure today that the date written on those reports is an exact date, a correct date?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
